questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Prior exposure and the asymmetry of a first epidemic
questions.learningObjective: explain why the age profile of a first epidemic differs from a recurring one
questions.stem: Two populations are of comparable size and roughly comparable means. One has had a disease for centuries, so most of those born into it meet it in infancy and survive; the other meets the disease for the first time inside a single generation. In the first population the deaths are concentrated at the extremes of age; in the second, a large share of the dead are adults in the middle of their working lives. Which feature explains the difference in the second population?

options.text: The whole population has no immune memory of the disease, so the infection finds susceptible hosts at every age instead of only where immunity has lapsed
The second population eats a poorer diet, so its malnutrition puts deaths at every age instead of at the extremes
options.misconception: attributes a difference in age profile to diet without any stated dietary difference

options.text: The first population keeps better records, so its apparent concentration at the extremes is an artefact of counting rather than of biology
options.misconception: explains a pattern by a recording habit with no evidence of one

options.text: The two outbreaks are different diseases, since the same illness is said to change its own symptoms on meeting a new population
options.misconception: supposes the pathogen changes species with its host

questions.explanation: The explanation is the composition of susceptibles rather than the food or the counting. In an old endemic population the disease is encountered in infancy, and a survivor's immunity is inherited by later children, so the adults who remain have all been through an infection; the deaths that persist are concentrated where immunity has lapsed or where the body cannot mount one, which is the young and the old. In a population meeting the disease for the first time, the susceptible fraction is the entire population, so the infection is not filtered by immunity at any age and the loss falls where the working population is largest. That difference matters historically for more than the head count, because a shock concentrated on adults removes the people who farm, fight, administer and reproduce, whereas one concentrated on children leaves the working order temporarily intact. The distractors each substitute an unrelated condition, a recording habit, or a change in the disease itself for the immune structure that is actually doing the work.
questions.hint: Ask what fraction of the population is susceptible in each case, and at what ages.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A vector that will not travel far from its breeding water
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a claim about how a disease arrives from a claim about how it then spreads
questions.stem: A fever reaches a port city in one summer. One party holds that the disease is local, generated in the city's own summer heat and standing water and brought on by a mosquito that does not travel far from the water in which it breeds. The other holds that the sickness is imported, carried in with the ships and the people in them, because it had been raging in the region the ships had just left. Which statement about the pair of claims is soundest?

options.text: The two claims are rivals, and the local claim must be false because the ships did arrive with fever cases aboard them
options.misconception: forces the two explanations to be exclusive

options.text: The two claims are rivals, and the imported claim is settled by the arrival of ships, since only a ship can carry a fever across the sea
options.misconception: assumes the answer in the word ship and never tests the alternative

options.text: The two claims are not rivals about the same thing, since an infected person can carry the agent into a mosquito population that was already breeding locally
The two claims are not rivals, because a mosquito that breeds locally cannot carry a disease that arrived from overseas
options.misconception: denies the very mechanism the two claims share

questions.explanation: The two claims have been framed as opposites when they describe two different links in one chain, and separating the links dissolves the disagreement. Importation asks how the agent first got into the district; local transmission asks how it then moves from person to person and from person to mosquito. Both can be true of the same summer, and the second is where the mosquito's short range does its work, because it means a local breeding population has to already be there for an arrival to be amplified. A party that insists on exclusivity is therefore committing itself to a stronger claim than the evidence can carry, either that no ships brought cases or that no local transmission occurred. The useful question is not which label is correct but which link the evidence bears on, and a mosquito that will not cross a district tells you about the second link and says nothing whatever about the first.
questions.hint: Ask what each claim is about: the arrival of the agent, or the spread of the agent once it has arrived.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A city's own return as a test of a claim about immunity
questions.learningObjective: assess a population claim against the counts the city itself kept

stimulus.body: From a return printed by a city council in the winter following an epidemic, recording the classes of the dead as they were entered by the district constables: 'Of the whole number of the dead, set down in the several wards and suburbs, we have entered those of the African descent apart from the rest, and the number so set apart is two hundred forty. The commissioners were told by physicians of the first rank that this people are by constitution not liable to the sickness, and upon that account no measure of the kind taken elsewhere was thought needful here. The truth of that opinion must now be looked for in the number itself, which is not small.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the return. A council's commissioners had been told that one population group in the city was not liable to the fever, and had therefore left it out of the measures applied to everyone else. The return states the opposite conclusion. Which statement about the two positions is soundest?

options.text: The claim was founded on clinical observation of the sick, so a council's arithmetic cannot bear on it and the return settles nothing
options.misconception: insists that only a physician's judgement can test a claim about constitution

options.text: The claim was a hypothesis about prior exposure that the city's own counts could have tested, and the test is reported here as failed, which is a different matter from the claim being doubted in advance
The return is a partisan document written to blame a population for a death toll, so its separate count is a rhetorical act and not evidence
options.misconception: reads motive in the document and dismisses the count it contains

options.text: The commissioner's conclusion settles the matter for good, so no later count of any kind need be kept
options.misconception: turns one count into a permanent exemption from further counting

questions.explanation: The return is valuable precisely because it closes an argument it is not supposed to close. The opinion the commissioners acted on was a claim about physiology that rested in the end on an assumption about prior exposure, and an assumption of that kind is checkable: if the group is not liable, its deaths should be near zero while the rest of the city is dying, and a city that counts its dead by district can look. The commissioners did the check, and the number they report is not small, so the measures they had exempted that population from should have been applied to it. Nothing here settles why the original opinion was held, and the tone of the passage shows they believed it, but a belief tested and contradicted is in a different condition from a belief merely doubted. The distractors each either insulate the claim from the check, dismiss the document for a motive, or over-read the result as a permanent exemption.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim the council acted on was the kind of claim that counts could test.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A carrier that cannot work in the heat
questions.learningObjective: explain how a temperature threshold can open or close a route for transmission
questions.stem: The rat flea is the carrier that matters in bubonic plague, and it is an inefficient carrier unless a colony of bacteria blocks its gut: with the gut blocked the flea regurgitates the organisms into whatever host it next bites, and with the gut open it simply excretes them and infects nobody. Laboratory and field work indicate that this blocking does not form above about 27 degrees C, and the sea and air temperatures along a stretch of coast between an endemic region and the Mediterranean are normally above that for most of the year. A study argues that the disease could not have crossed that stretch in a normal year, and that it could in a year when regional temperatures were several degrees below the norm for long enough. Which conclusion does the mechanism license?

options.text: Cooling would produce the disease in the region it affected, since the carrier's behaviour alone determines whether disease exists
options.misconception: makes a necessary condition sufficient and invents a source of the pathogen

options.text: The constraint shows that the disease was never present across that stretch, since a constraint that held for centuries cannot be broken by a few decades
options.misconception: assumes that a long-standing constraint cannot be temporarily lifted

options.text: The mechanism is irrelevant to how the disease arrived, since transmission and arrival are decided entirely by shipping
options.misconception: declares the mechanism irrelevant to the question it is offered to explain

options.text: Cooling of a particular kind, in a particular stretch of sea, would relax a constraint that normally holds, so a climate change can be a necessary enabling condition without being a sufficient cause

questions.explanation: What the threshold supplies is a necessary condition, and the item tests whether you can keep that distinction straight. The fever requires a carrier that transmits efficiently, and efficiency requires a gut blocked by a colony, and the colony requires a temperature regime that the crossing normally does not have. Lower the temperature for long enough and the requirement is met, so climate becomes the sort of thing that has to go right before the disease can pass, which is a real causal role and not a decorative one. But enabling is not producing: the threshold explains why a route was available, not where the organism came from, and a study that shows the route opened has not shown the traveller. The third distractor makes a historical error of a familiar kind, treating a normally closed door as proof that the door has never opened, and the fourth denies the relevance of a mechanism that is directly about transmission.
questions.hint: Ask what the temperature threshold has to be true for, and what it does not by itself establish.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A livestock plague that widened the range of a human disease
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which an animal epidemic moved a human one
questions.stem: The steps by which a cattle disease in East Africa in the late 1880s is connected to an epidemic of a human disease carried by the fly that breeds in bush are set out below. Place them in the order in which they had to happen.

options.text: The herds die, and a society that had organised itself around the care and movement of cattle loses the basis on which it used the country's grassland
The grazing that had kept the country open stops where the herders have gone, and the thicket in which the fly breeds closes over the same ground they are now using
Herders who can no longer keep cattle turn to hunting and gathering, and take up country they had previously gone out of their way to avoid
People are now living and travelling in the country where the fly breeds, and a human disease carried by that fly spreads through the districts it now occupies

questions.explanation: The order is a chain in which each step is a precondition of the next. The herds die first, because everything else depends on the loss of the herds and on nothing else. The herders then move into the country they had avoided, and that move is a response to the loss rather than a cause of the disease, which is why the sequence runs this way and not with the movement first. Only after they are there does the third step occur in the form the argument needs, because the grazing that had kept the country open stops where they have gone and the thicket in which the fly breeds closes over the ground they are now using, so the people and the fly arrive in the same country together. Only then can a fly-borne human disease spread there, and the final step is a consequence of the two middle ones. The point of the ordering is that no step involves one pathogen passing to another, which is what distinguishes this chain from a direct transmission claim.
questions.hint: Ask which step is a response to the loss of the herds, and which is a consequence of the herders' response.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A quarantine that protected a crop and broke a herd economy
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the aim of a control measure from its effect on the people it was applied to
questions.stem: In a colony whose grazing economies depend on moving herds between seasonal water, officials order that herds be held still, fenced, and separated, and that animals crossing a boundary be shot. A veterinary report concludes that the measure halted the advance of the disease. A study of the affected districts concludes that the herds' owners were ruined, that the rules were applied unevenly, and that a population of herders became a population of labourers. Which statement about the pair of conclusions is soundest?

options.text: The two conclusions contradict each other, so one of the two reports must be mistaken about the sequence of events
options.misconception: refuses to let an aim and an effect be evaluated separately

options.text: The second conclusion is the stronger, since a measure that ruins a population cannot have been effective against the disease it was aimed at
options.misconception: lets a consequence settle the question of biological effectiveness

options.text: The two conclusions are compatible, since a measure can be effective against a disease and destructive of the economy that made the affected population mobile, and effectiveness at the first is not evidence against the second
The two conclusions are both about the economy, since a veterinary report in a colonial archive can only be measuring prices
options.misconception: misdescribes what a veterinary report is competent to measure

questions.explanation: A control measure has an efficacy question and a consequence question, and they are answered by different evidence, which is why two competent studies can report the same intervention without agreeing. The veterinary report is competent about transmission and is in a position to know how the disease moved; the study of the districts is competent about what happened to herders whose survival strategy was movement, and is in a position to count households, wages and departures. The honest reading is that the policy did what it was designed to do and something else besides, and neither competence cancels the other. Notice also that uneven enforcement is a third fact rather than a contradiction of the first two, since a rule applied to some herders and not others changes who bears the cost without changing the rule's design. The distractors each force an exclusivity the situation does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what each report is in a position to know, and what it is not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Weakening a germ to make a vaccine
questions.learningObjective: explain why an effective vaccine could be built from the same organism that causes the disease
questions.stem: The first attempts to protect against a cattle plague used material taken from animals that had recovered: the blood or serum of survivors was given to animals at risk and it did not protect them. A workable vaccine was found only after the organism was carried repeatedly through an animal species it does not normally infect, until it had changed enough to be harmless while still provoking the response that protects. Which feature of the second method is essential to it?

options.text: Survivors carry the protective quality in their blood, so the material works wherever it is taken from a recovered animal
options.misconception: restates the approach the sequence reports as failing

options.text: Successive passage changes the organism itself, so what is given is a weakened relative of the cause rather than something drawn from a recovered animal
An abnormal host is chosen because its blood is purer, so the effect comes from the host rather than from the organism
options.misconception: credits the host rather than the changed organism

options.text: Repeated passage makes the organism stronger, so the vaccine works by giving the animals a mild case from which they recover
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change that the method depends on

questions.explanation: The method is called attenuation, and the whole of it lies in the fact that the material given is still the same species of thing as the cause, just altered by its own history of replication. That is why a survivor's blood fails: the protective state after recovery is a state of the animal, produced by an immune response, and there is no reason at all for it to be transferable, and the early failures are exactly what you would predict from a theory that says immunity is a property of the individual. Carrying the organism through an unfamiliar host changes the selection acting on it, so what eventually reaches the vaccinated animal is a strain that no longer kills efficiently and still triggers the same defensive response, which is the property a vaccine has to have. Distinction worth holding: the aim is not to remove the organism but to remove its danger, and the change is in the organism's own properties rather than in the recipient's.
questions.hint: Ask what the material in the syringe is, and how it came to be that.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reservoir that eradication has to remove
questions.learningObjective: state what distinguishes a disease that can be eradicated from one that cannot
questions.stem: A human disease has been driven out of most countries by vaccinating people and by finding and isolating cases quickly. A second disease affecting both people and animals was declared eradicated globally after a campaign of about a decade, and it is the only animal disease so far to be so declared. Which feature distinguishes the second from a disease that persists in a wild reservoir and can therefore be reintroduced?

options.text: The organism is so fragile in the open air that it cannot survive in a port, so a boundary is enough to keep it out
options.misconception: supplies a property of the organism that is not what makes eradication possible

options.text: The disease is too rare to be noticed, so a few unnoticed cases are needed to re-establish it and the problem is one of reporting
options.misconception: makes rarity rather than the absence of a reservoir the difficulty

options.text: The disease moves too quickly for a campaign to follow, so eradication depended on treating animals rather than people
options.misconception: reverses the roles of the two kinds of population that can be reached

options.text: The organism has no reservoir outside the populations that vaccination can reach, so interrupting transmission in those populations removes it rather than merely suppressing it

questions.explanation: Eradication and control are different achievements and the difference is about where the organism can sit between outbreaks. A disease that lives in a wild reservoir, whether rodents in a particular terrain or organisms in soil, can always be reintroduced into a vaccinated population by a traveller, an imported animal or a wind-blown particle, and every effort therefore has to be repeated forever, which is what control means. A disease with no such refuge can be taken below the threshold at which transmission sustains itself, and once that happens it cannot come back on its own, which is why the declaration of eradication is a one-off achievement and a reason to vaccinate animals and not only people. The confusion this item is aimed at is the common one that treats the disappearance of a disease from a country as the same as its disappearance from the world, and the two differ by precisely the existence of the reservoir.
questions.hint: Ask where the organism can wait when nobody is vaccinating, and whether that place can be reached.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deliberate infection as a controlled gamble
questions.learningObjective: explain why an accepted risk can be preferable to an unbounded one
questions.stem: Before any vaccine existed, a practice developed in which material was taken from the pustule of a person with a mild case and introduced into the arm of a healthy person, in the hope of causing a mild infection that would protect against a severe one afterwards. It was widely used, and it was also known to kill a small number of the people who underwent it, and doctors argued about the exchange for years before the practice was overtaken by vaccination. Which statement best describes the reasoning of those who defended it?

options.text: The material was thought to be free of risk because the disease was caught at its mildest from a person who had already recovered
options.misconception: denies the risk that defenders of the practice themselves conceded

options.text: A small known risk of dying was preferred to a large uncertain risk of dying, because the outcome of catching the disease was both likelier and far worse, and the risk that was taken was the smaller of the two
The practice was defended as a religious duty, since several communities held that a person's body must be opened to a disease the community knew
options.misconception: explains a medical judgement by a motive the arguments do not mention

options.text: The practice was defended because it was cheaper than the isolation it replaced, so the argument was about cost and never about risk at all
options.misconception: reduces a disputed exchange to a budget question

questions.explanation: The defenders' position was a comparison, not a denial: given that an outbreak would otherwise kill a far larger number, a procedure that kills a small, knowable fraction of those who accept it is an improvement, and a doctor who denied that was denying arithmetic rather than making a medical point. What the exchange required was information, since the argument only works if the risk taken is genuinely small and genuinely knowable, and that is what the century-long argument was actually about, since earlier practice drew the material from people with the severe form, which converted a modest gamble into a large one. Once a method existed that produced protection without producing the disease at all, the comparison no longer favoured the gamble, and the practice was abandoned rather than argued out of existence, which is a good indication that the argument had been about relative risks all along.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two risks actually was, and which was larger.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a laboratory demonstration settles and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the scope of a controlled demonstration from the scope of a general claim
questions.stem: In the 1870s and 1880s a laboratory reported a set of controlled experiments in which material from one species, weakened by heating, protected animals of another species against an organism that killed them, and the report was read as establishing that the material could prevent the disease. The experiments were repeated and extended. Which statement about the standing of the result is soundest?

options.text: The demonstrations establish the claim in general, because a controlled experiment that works once works everywhere
options.misconception: concedes nothing to the difference between a demonstration and a use

options.text: The demonstrations establish nothing at all, because a laboratory result cannot settle a question about a disease in a whole population
options.misconception: dismisses a controlled result on the ground of its setting

options.text: The demonstrations establish the claim only until someone repeats them, so their standing depends on the number of repetitions rather than on their design
options.misconception: measures a result by how often it was repeated rather than how well it was made

options.text: The demonstrations establish that the treatment can protect under controlled conditions, and what they cannot establish is how far the protection extends in practice, which is a separate question requiring other evidence

questions.explanation: The discipline this item asks for is separating a proposition from the conditions that make it true, and the laboratory result is a proposition with stated conditions: this material, weakened this way, given to an animal of this kind, protected it against this organism. It is a strong result, stronger than an opinion or a correlation, and it is exactly the sort of thing a controlled demonstration is for. What it does not carry is the whole of the practical claim, which adds questions of dose, of timing, of how many doses, of how long the protection lasts, and of what happens in a population where nobody is in a laboratory, and each of those is a separate question with its own evidence. A student who treats the general claim as already proven will not know which of those questions to ask next, and a student who treats the result as worthless will miss the one thing it actually established.
questions.hint: Ask what the experiment varied and held fixed, and what the general claim adds to that.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the last case is the hardest to find
questions.learningObjective: explain why the final stage of an eradication campaign is different from the bulk of it
questions.stem: In the final stage of a global campaign against a disease, teams stop vaccinating most of a population and instead search for every case, trace every contact, and vaccinate the contacts around it. Officials note that this stage consumed most of the campaign's resources and that it failed completely in some countries. Which feature of this stage explains both the expense and the failure?

options.text: The contacts of a case are harder to vaccinate than the general population, since a general population is self-selecting and contacts are not
options.misconception: supplies a difference in the people that is not the source of the cost

options.text: Rare diseases mutate faster, so the vaccine stops working at low levels of prevalence and a new strain takes over
options.misconception: invents a mechanism the sequence does not mention

options.text: Once a disease is rare, each case is a separate event requiring a search and a response, so the effort required rises exactly as the number of cases falls
The search requires laboratories that small countries cannot afford, so the failures are explained by the distribution of wealth
options.misconception: reduces a known feature of the method to a claim about money

questions.explanation: The shape of the effort is set by a ratio, and the ratio inverts at the end of the campaign. While a disease is common, one visit to a district that vaccinate most of the people present protects most of the people present, and the cost per person protected is low and falling. Once a disease is rare, the same protection requires knowing where the handful of cases were, who they met, and when, and that knowledge has to be actively sought rather than gathered by walking into a village, because the cases are not where you would expect them. The last case in a district can cost more than the whole mass campaign that preceded it, and a country in which the case rate was always low and scattered is exactly the country in which the method's assumption, that cases are discoverable by contact, is hardest to satisfy. That is the structural problem, and it is why the last stage looks like an inversion of the first.
questions.hint: Ask what the teams had to know, and how that knowledge changes as the case rate falls.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A town's method that became the world standard
questions.learningObjective: trace a local administrative innovation into a later international programme

stimulus.body: From a paper read before a society of medical officers of health in the early 1900s by the officer responsible for one English town: 'It will be well understood that no reliance is placed upon general vaccination as a safeguard. The method here described is set out in full so that others may judge of it. Every case of smallpox is notified to me as it occurs. The patient is at once removed to a hospital where the nurses and the laundry are under control. The contacts of the sick person are traced, kept apart from the public for the full period of the incubation, and vaccinated at once. A house is not released until the contacts have been seen through. The result in this town has been that the disease is seldom seen, and when it is seen it is seen in small numbers.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the paper. A local health officer describes a method his town used and disclaims reliance on general vaccination. Decades later, the strategy adopted for a global campaign against the same disease is to find each case and vaccinate the people around it rather than to vaccinate the whole population. Which statement about the relationship between the two is best supported?

options.text: The two are the same method, and the global campaign adopted the local officer's insight that protection concentrated around each case is what makes the last cases findable
The two are unrelated, since a global campaign must be built from laboratory science and cannot owe anything to a town's experience
options.misconception: makes a requirement of method that neither programme needed

options.text: The two are the same method, and the local officer's disclaimer of vaccination is what makes the claim true, since a method that works without a vaccine is necessarily superior
options.misconception: takes a disclaimer of credit as a demonstration of superiority

options.text: The two are related only by the accident of timing, since a small town and a world organisation have no way to exchange findings
options.misconception: denies communication between a published paper and a later programme

questions.explanation: The method in the extract is built from four commitments: notification of every case, isolation of the patient, tracing of contacts, and vaccination of the contacts. Each of them concentrates effort near a case rather than distributing it evenly, and the last two are exactly what a global campaign later adopted, with the addition of a laboratory test to confirm the case. The local officer's disclaimer is worth reading carefully rather than as a boast: he is saying that his town did not depend on high general uptake, which is a claim about what his town achieved, and it is a claim that leaves his town vulnerable if the method is interrupted, which is the well-known weakness of the approach. What makes the item interesting is not the priority of the inventor but the structure: a method devised for a town of a few hundred thousand, and found to fit a population of hundreds of millions.
questions.hint: Ask which of the officer's four commitments the global campaign also adopted.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a town's low death toll does and does not show
questions.learningObjective: weigh the competing explanations of a favourable local record
questions.stem: One English town recorded unusually few smallpox deaths through a period when neighbouring towns recorded many, and the town's medical officer reported that general vaccination had fallen sharply after a change in its local government. A study of the period finds that most adults in the town had nevertheless been vaccinated earlier, that the town had notification and a fever hospital, and that it had quarantined contacts. Which account best fits the record?

options.text: The low toll shows that general vaccination is unnecessary, since the town managed with case finding alone after uptake fell
options.misconception: isolates one component and ignores the inherited protection that preceded it

options.text: The town combined a high inherited level of protection with active case finding, so the low toll shows what the combination achieves and does not isolate the value of either part, nor the effect of losing general uptake later
The low toll shows that the vaccine works, since the only town with few deaths was the town where the most people had been vaccinated as children
options.misconception: asserts the control that the record's own alternative prevents

options.text: The low toll shows that the disease was milder that year everywhere, since the town's neighbour recorded many deaths in the same months
options.misconception: explains a difference between neighbours by a factor common to both

questions.explanation: The town is a hard case because several things were true of it at once, and the record cannot separate them without a comparison the case does not provide. By the time general uptake fell, a large share of the adults in the town had already been vaccinated, and a partly protected adult population is a very different starting point from an entirely susceptible one; the fall in general uptake therefore says little about what a town would look like if nobody had ever been vaccinated. Set against that, notification, a hospital and contact isolation are all in the record, and each of them independently reduces deaths. The correct conclusion is the modest one: the combination works, this case cannot apportion credit between its parts, and it says nothing about the counterfactual in which the early protection was absent. The fourth option is a reminder that a common cause is usually the first thing to exclude and the last thing to assert.
questions.hint: Ask what the town's starting point was before the thing that changed, and what else was in place.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A legal category and the record it creates
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a right to refuse becomes a usable record
questions.stem: A law of the later nineteenth century creates a formal category of person who may lawfully refuse a treatment a parent has been ordered to have administered to a child. The consequences of that change arrive in a recognisable order. Put them in that order.

options.text: Organised groups of parents begin to use the category, and officials find their correspondence and their legal business growing beyond what they had to deal with before
The new register is inspected and found to be growing faster than the returns of treatments actually administered, which is reported upward as a burden on the administration
A parent may refuse in a form the law recognises, and a magistrate is required to enter that refusal in a register kept for the purpose
A historian finds a series of refusals in a form a series of silent absences could never have produced, and can count them by district and by year

questions.explanation: The order runs from the law to the register to the use of the register, and each step is what makes the next one possible. The category has to exist and be enforceable before anybody can act on it, so the requirement that a magistrate enter a refusal is first, and that requirement is also what makes the refusal a written act rather than a private one. Which feature of the design does most to strengthen the inference that the treatment caused the difference?

options.misconception: supplies a selection rule that would make the comparison worse rather than better

options.text: The teams were sent by an outside foundation, so their counting was not influenced by anyone who benefited from the result
options.misconception: credits the identity of the counters rather than the design of the comparison

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A stated aim and the effect that was measured
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between a programme's purpose and the outcome it produced
questions.stem: A programme against a fly-borne disease sprayed the interior walls of houses with a persistent insecticide, year after year, in a district where the fly bred in the bush around the houses. Officials reported a sharp fall in cases in the years when spraying was carried out and a rise in the intervals between campaigns, and they described the aim as the interruption of transmission. Explain why the measured effect and the stated aim are not the same thing, and what the rise between campaigns shows.

The insecticide is laid on a wall, and a fly that is resting on the wall is killed, so the number of bites a household receives falls and the case count falls with it. The fly, however, breeds in the bush, and the population that breeds there is untouched by the spraying, so what has been achieved is a reduction in the number of flies near people rather than a reduction in the capacity of the species to replace them. That is a different quantity from the one the programme set out to change, and it is measurable in a different way: interruption of transmission requires the population to be held below the level at which a new infection is likely to be met by a susceptible carrier, whereas fewer bites is a reduction in the rate at which households are exposed, which can be undone by a single season without spraying. The rise between campaigns is the evidence that settles which of the two was achieved. A reversible effect is a suppression: whatever the spraying changes is restored as soon as it stops, and the only way to tell a permanent change from a temporary one is to stop applying the treatment and see whether the effect persists. Since it does not persist, the programme should be described as having reduced exposure while it was running, and as having had no effect on the conditions that sustain the disease, which is also why later programmes against the same disease placed much more weight on removing breeding sites and on killing a stage of the life cycle other than the adult one being sprayed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A campaign that changed its own objective
questions.learningObjective: explain what happens when a time-limited goal proves unreachable

stimulus.body: From the report of the director of a regional health organisation to its governing body in the middle of the twentieth century: 'The Programme was set up in 1955 with a stated term, and the term is the point of it. A disease is to be extinguished within a fixed period, and the period is what has driven the work, since work that must end can be planned, budgeted and checked. On the evidence now before us the extinction of the disease in the countries where it is most firmly established cannot be achieved by the methods available, and the attempt has consumed the greater part of the funds and staff. I recommend that the Programme cease to be a campaign with a term and become a service without one. The recommendation is not a defeat. What is proposed is the removal of a date from the heading of a document, and the consequence will be that the work must now be judged by what it sustains rather than by what it concludes.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the report. An organisation proposes to give up a fixed-term campaign and become an open-ended service, arguing that this is not a defeat. Which statement about the reasoning is best supported?

options.text: The reasoning is a rhetorical device, since abandoning a dated goal is always presented as a redefinition of success and never as a reduction in ambition
options.misconception: treats the framing as a manoeuvre and rules out the possibility it is accurate

options.text: The reasoning treats success as having been defined by a deadline that cannot be met, so replacing the deadline with a duty to sustain the work changes what counts as achievement without changing what is done
The reasoning is sound only if the disease has in fact been extinguished, since nothing needs sustaining once the work is finished
options.misconception: makes the proposal conditional on the very outcome it is designed to accommodate

options.text: The reasoning is a defence of the organisation's record, since a fixed term that ends without success is worse for the director than one that never had a term
options.misconception: reduces an institutional judgement to the career interest of its author

questions.explanation: The report's move is worth reading closely, because the last sentence is the whole of its argument. A campaign with a term is judged on whether the term produced the stated result, and a body that has failed on that test has no defensible position; a service without a term is judged on whether the thing it is responsible for continues to function, which is a different and indefinitely renewable question. The recommendation therefore does not reduce the ambition, and it does not conceal a failure, since the evidence about the methods is stated plainly in the paragraph above. What changes is the criterion, and the reason it has to change is that a criterion with a date attached to it must be answered with a yes or a no, and the honest answer to the first is no. That is a real pattern in the history of international health, and it is worth recognising because it changes what the documents mean.
questions.hint: Ask what the two arrangements make an organisation accountable for.

questions.topic: Repeated treatment and the population it selects
questions.learningObjective: explain how a repeated control measure can change the thing it is applied to
questions.stem: A control programme sprays the same insecticide on the same walls every season for a decade, in a district where the vector breeds in the surrounding bush. After several years the spray reduces the number of flies killed per unit of spray, and the programme responds by increasing the dose, the frequency, and eventually the number of compounds tried. Which feature of this sequence best explains the change in the number killed per unit of spray?

options.text: The spray loses its potency as it ages, so the number killed falls because the compound decays while it waits for the next season
options.misconception: invents a storage explanation the sequence does not mention

options.text: The flies have learned to avoid the treated houses, so the number killed falls because the behaviour of the population has changed
options.misconception: supposes learning where a heritable susceptibility is what is being selected

options.text: The number killed has not changed at all, since the flies that survive are the young ones and the population as a whole is unaltered
options.misconception: denies a compositional shift that the programme's own response presupposes

options.text: The spray removes the individuals that are most susceptible and leaves those that survive, so each season the population is more resistant than the last and the same spray kills a smaller share of it

questions.explanation: A control measure applied without variation is a selection pressure, and the population it acts on responds the way any population responds to selection: the individuals least affected are the ones that reproduce, and they pass on what made them less affected. That is why the sequence of responses in the case is a escalating one, more, more often, more compounds, and each step buys a shorter period of usefulness. It also explains why the fix is not a bigger dose: the trait being selected for is resistance to the compound, so raising the dose selects for it again, and the only durable answers are variation in what is used, or removing the breeding sites where the population lives, or killing a stage of the life cycle that is not the one being selected for.

options.misconception: assumes an unbroken hidden presence rather than testing a repeated introduction

options.text: The shipping explains the spread between ports but not the recurrence, since recurrence requires the organism to survive somewhere between voyages
options.misconception: denies the survival that any maintenance of the organism must involve

options.text: A regular connection can carry the agent into a port and a port can hold it, so a network of such ports behaves as a single large district with many entrances
The pattern says nothing about shipping, since a disease present in many ports at once points to a common origin in one of them
options.misconception: reads simultaneity as proof of a single source and ignores repeated travel

At that point the number of introductions per year across the network becomes the relevant quantity, and a network with a dozen linked ports has a far lower chance of a long quiet interval than an isolated island does. questions.hint: Ask what a port with ships in it provides, and what the network of such ports does with them.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why recovery from a mortality shock is slow
questions.learningObjective: explain the demographic shape of a population recovering from a one-off shock
questions.stem: Explain why a population that has suffered a single severe mortality shock takes several generations to return to its former size, and why a population exposed to the same shock repeatedly does not behave the same way.

answer.exemplar: A single shock removes people from every age at once, and the age structure that remains is the structure that decides what happens next. Where the shock cut adults hardest, the survivors are disproportionately the young and the old, the number of people in the reproductive ages is small, and births therefore fall even though the survivors have food and are not themselves ill. A smaller number of women of childbearing age means fewer births; fewer births means the population cannot climb back for as long as it takes for the large cohort of survivors to reach the reproductive ages, which is a generation, and usually longer because the number that does reach it was itself reduced. The arithmetic of this is simply that a population replaces its members by reproduction, so the rate of recovery is governed by the size of the fertile cohort rather than by the number of survivors. A population exposed to shocks repeatedly behaves differently because the selection is repeated: the survivors of each shock are disproportionately those whose constitution let them through, and after several rounds the age distribution and the constitution of the surviving population are both different from those of any population that has escaped them. That is why the two cases must be described in different terms, and why a figure for the size of a shock says very little about how long its consequences last.

stimulus.body: Extract from a study of annual tree-ring series from many sites across the northern hemisphere: 'The years 536 and the early 540s appear in the records as years of exceptionally narrow rings, and the same years appear in series from sites whose soils, species and climates have nothing in common with one another. The 536 layer is matched by ice from the north and the later layer by ice from both poles, which is the pattern expected of an eruption outside the northern hemisphere in the second case. Neither layer is large enough to account for the whole of the cooling; together they are. We note that the second deposit carried more aerosol to the stratosphere than the eruption of 1815, which is the largest in the last two thousand years.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

options.misconception: cuts the record off at the first event and discards the second

options.text: The sulphate layers prove the eruptions were large enough, so the growth anomaly in the trees must have some cause other than climate
options.misconception: treats a physical deposit as a substitute for a climatic link

options.text: The northern and southern ice shows the eruptions were simultaneous, since deposits at both poles can only form at the same time
options.misconception: infers simultaneity from the existence of deposits at both poles

Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.misconception: assumes the worst-hit district is the first to starve

options.text: The difference lies in the weather afterwards, since a cold spring in the following year decides whether the hungry survive
options.misconception: locates the whole difference in a second year's weather

options.misconception: treats uniformity as security without noticing what it removes

options.text: The region's yields have risen, so the risk of famine has fallen in proportion to the rise in yield per acre
options.misconception: confuses a rise in average yield with a fall in the variance of the harvest

options.text: The region's food supply now depends on a single organism, so a pathogen that reaches that organism can depress the harvest across the whole region at once

options.text: The candidates are not rivals, since a famine is by definition a failure of food supply and the supply was adequate

Which statement about the objection is best supported?

options.misconception: restates the supply-versus-access confusion as a definition

Which reading of that policy is best supported?

options.misconception: attributes the scale of a policy to one cause the text does not name

options.misconception: infers a delay from the existence of a code without evidence about timing

options.text: The rules institutionalised a judgement about how much relief to give, so the policy's severity was a chosen quantity inside an administrative framework rather than a simple measure of the shortage

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A code that assumes a household it does not describe
questions.learningObjective: assess the household model built into a rule

stimulus.body: From a famine code issued by a colonial administration in the last decades of the nineteenth century, section on the assessment of need: 'Entitlement to relief shall be determined by the officer in charge of the district, who shall proceed from the average consumption of the inhabitants of the district, as returned in the last settlement, and shall deduct from that average the quantity of food which the household might reasonably be expected to have grown for itself. Where the cultivators of a village are found to be in debt to the zamindar or the money-lender, and the debt exceeds the value of their standing crop, they shall be treated as destitute. The test is to be applied to the village and not to the household, in order that the proceedings may not be multiplied.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the section. Which feature of the section is most likely to produce a systematic error in the count of people needing relief?

options.text: The test is applied to a village rather than a household, which will always undercount in a village of unequal households and always overcount in a village of equal ones
options.misconception: states a direction of bias that depends on the village and the rule supplies no such direction

options.text: The test of need is worked out from a district average of consumption and a household's own expected production, which assumes the average is a fair starting point when a bad year removes the very harvest that made it fair
The test treats as destitute only those in debt, so a family that is hungry and free of debt will be found not to need relief however little it has
options.misconception: reads a condition of indebtedness as though it were the sole criterion of need

options.text: The test is settled by an officer in charge, so any error in it is a matter of that officer's competence rather than of the rule's construction
options.misconception: locates every possible error in the administrator rather than in the design

questions.explanation: The interesting thing about this section is that it is a careful document that still carries a structural risk, and identifying that risk is the whole exercise. It measures need as a gap between what a person consumes normally and what they might grow, which is a serviceable definition in an ordinary year, because the district average and the local crop are then both reasonable proxies. In a year when the harvest fails, the second term collapses toward zero for exactly the people the rule is meant to find, and the first term is itself a memory of normal times, so the computed gap is both measured against a world that has stopped existing and is then multiplied by a district average that smooths away the differences the gap depends on. The result is a count that is defensible in form and wrong in direction, and the direction of the error is what a reader should be able to state without being told.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule uses as a baseline, and what happens to that baseline in a bad year.

The third year of the outbreak: 'buried within the year, 61, of whom 34 within the quarter ending at Candlemas'. A note in the same hand on a separate leaf: 'the sexton hath this year interred many of the parish in the churchyard without the book's entry, by his own reckoning, and the churchwardens have charged him for it.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the account. A study uses this book to claim that the outbreak killed about seven per cent of the town's population. Which statement about the claim is best supported?

options.text: The book is a complete record, since the churchwarden entered every burial and the discrepancy arises from a dispute about the price of the service
options.misconception: supposes a disagreement about fees where the text records missed entries

options.text: The book is useless, since a series with one year of anomaly cannot be used to establish anything about a town
options.misconception: rules out the use of a series because part of it is striking

options.text: The book supports a figure of about seven per cent, since a parish of about 900 with 61 burials in the year would give that figure and the parish can be counted elsewhere
options.misconception: assumes the one known omission is the only omission in the series

options.text: The book can establish that recorded burials rose sharply and when in the year they occurred, and it cannot on its own establish a total for the parish, because a known class of interments was kept out of the book

The second is a total for the parish, and that is exactly what the note destroys: the sexton has recorded, in the same hand and the same book, that a class of interments was performed without an entry. A mortality rate is a ratio with a denominator, and the omission sits in the numerator, so the figure the study computes is a floor and its error has a known sign. The useful conclusion is the narrow one, and the fourth option shows precisely the mistake, which is to treat one documented omission as though it were the only one.

questions.learningObjective: identify the systematic gap in a weekly record of deaths

options.misconception: infers absence of deaths from absence of records

options.text: A shared gap shows that the two series are the same document copied twice, since only copying produces identical omissions
options.misconception: supplies a single cause where several ordinary causes are available

options.text: A shared gap shows that the epidemic paused, since a disease that stopped killed nobody and therefore left nothing to record
options.misconception: takes an administrative gap for a biological one

questions.explanation: The coincidence is the evidence, and its direction matters: two offices keeping books for different purposes, under different authority, with different obligations, both have nothing in the same weeks. questions.stem: A surgeon writes that a ship's crew lost eight men to a fever during a voyage, that the ship carried ninety-four men besides officers, and that the disease was contracted in a particular harbour. options.misconception: mistakes a single observed ratio for an estimated rate

options.text: The figure covers the voyage, since a surgeon attending a ship is present for the whole of the ship's company and its passengers
options.misconception: assumes the observer's coverage was complete

options.text: The figure is a count of deaths among people the surgeon attended on one voyage, and a study needs to say how such a count is related to the crews of the many other voyages before it can be used as a rate

questions.hint: Ask who is inside the count and who is outside it, and whether the omissions are random.

questions.topic: An age that bone does not give
questions.learningObjective: state what skeletal evidence supports and what it does not
questions.stem: A burial ground yields a number of skeletons, and a study reports an average age at death of thirty-one years, derived from the condition of the joints, the density of the bone and the degree of wear on the teeth. Which statement about that figure is best supported?

options.text: The figure is the average age of the population, since a burial ground holds one of every death in the community and so gives the population's age structure
options.misconception: assumes complete coverage of the deaths in a community

options.text: The figure is an estimate for the individuals examined, and a grave that was not dug, a body that did not reach it, or a person buried elsewhere will not appear in it at all
The figure is a measure of life expectancy, since an average age at death in a series of graves is the length of life the living could expect
options.misconception: confuses a mean age at death with a life expectancy at birth

options.text: The figure is precise, since the three methods of estimation are independent and their agreement settles the matter
options.misconception: supposes that several indicators cannot share a bias

questions.explanation: Skeletal age estimation is a genuine and useful discipline, but its output is bounded in a way that is easy to lose sight of. The methods are indicators of a physiological process whose pace varies between individuals, between periods and between populations, so the figure is an estimate with an uncertainty, and the three indicators are not independent witnesses: they can all be pushed the same way by a diet, a workload or a disease that leaves its mark on bone and teeth together. More important is what the estimate is about. It is an average for the skeletons that were examined, and every stage between the community and the examination is a filter: who was buried there rather than elsewhere, whose bones survived, and which of those the excavation sampled. An average for the sample is a real datum, but a long way from a population's average, and the difference is not noise to be reported as a margin of error.
questions.hint: Ask who is in the sample, and what had to happen for a person to be in it.

questions.learningObjective: assess retrospective diagnosis as a historical method
questions.stem: A chronicle of the sixth century describes a sickness by its appearance: fever, swellings under the skin, blackening of the flesh, and death in a few days. A later study identifies the disease as the one that caused a pandemic, on the strength of those descriptions and of genetic evidence from graves dated to the period. Which statement about the identification is best supported?

options.misconception: makes one kind of evidence decisive by stipulation

options.text: The identification is settled by the descriptions, since a chronicle written at the time is closer to the events than anything a laboratory can produce
options.misconception: prefers proximity as a general rule for identification

options.text: The identification is a modern convenience, since calling the sickness by a modern name is a category mistake that no careful historian should make
options.misconception: declares all retrospective naming illegitimate, which is most of what medicine and history do

options.text: The identification rests on a chain of separate propositions, each with its own failure mode, so the strength of the conclusion is the strength of the weakest link and the chain should be stated as such

The distractors each pick a single link and treat the whole as settled, which is the way such claims usually go wrong in popular writing.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true at each step between a chronicle's words and a laboratory's finding.

questions.topic: A case, an outbreak, and an epidemic
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the standard terms for the scale of an occurrence
questions.stem: Three reports are filed on the same disease. The first records a single household in which two people were ill. The second records eleven cases within one village over five weeks. The third records cases across four provinces for two years, with deaths in every month of the period. Which statement about the terms in use is correct?

options.misconception: dismisses a distinction that carries real information

options.text: The conclusion is unsafe because the average is unreliable, since a four-year average cannot be distinguished from a random number, so the year's figure proves nothing at all

options.text: A dose count is a count of doses given, so it has to be divided by a figure for the number of eligible people, and that figure is the part of the record the campaign was least likely to hold
A list of places reached establishes that a team was present in a district, which is not the same as a statement about how many people were vaccinated there
A case notification is a report made by somebody who found a case, so a low notification count is evidence about reporting at least as much as about disease
A high dose count in a district proves the campaign succeeded there, since the number given is the number needed to achieve the aim
options.misconception: treats a measure of effort as a measure of the result

options.text: The absence of records for a district shows that the campaign did not operate there, since a campaign that ran would have left a file
options.misconception: reads absence of a file as absence of activity

questions.explanation: The three defensible statements share a single idea, which is that every number in a campaign record is a count of something other than what the argument wants. Doses given are not doses received, and not doses needed, and the denominator that would convert the first into the second is a population figure the campaign may never have held. A place list is a record of movements by the campaign, which is evidence about effort and nothing about coverage. A notification is an act of finding, so a district with a good health service reports more cases than a district with a poor one, and the direction of that bias is consistent and predictable. The two indefensible statements make the two classic errors: reading an input as an output, and reading a missing file as a missing activity, when the likeliest explanation for a district with no file is that its administration kept no file.
questions.hint: Ask of each figure what was actually counted when it was entered.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An identification that settles a different question than the one asked
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what an identification of a pathogen settles from what it leaves open
questions.stem: For the pandemics of the fourteenth and sixth centuries, the organism responsible was eventually identified by analysing genetic material from skeletal remains of victims dated to the periods in question, after a long dispute in which the cause had been argued from symptoms, from the pattern of spread, and from accounts of rats and of person-to-person transmission. Which statement about the result of that identification is best supported?

options.text: It settled both the identity and the mechanism, since an organism cannot be transmitted except by the means its biology requires
options.misconception: assumes a mechanism follows from an identity without stating what it would be

options.text: It settled what the disease was, and it left the mechanism of transmission open, since identifying the organism does not by itself show how it reached the people who died of it
It settled nothing, since a genome recovered from a skeleton is a sequence and not a diagnosis of the symptoms the chronicles describe
options.misconception: dismisses a strong result because of the form the evidence takes

options.text: It settled the mechanism and left the identity open, since transmission can be carried by several organisms and one of them was always the likelier
options.misconception: reverses the two things the evidence addressed

questions.explanation: The distinction is between naming the thing and describing the route, and a great deal of confused argument comes from sliding between them. Recovering the organism's genetic material from remains of the right date settles a question that had been argued for a long time on indirect grounds, and it does so in the strongest possible form, material from the victims themselves. What it does not do is show how the organism got from where it lives to a person's bloodstream, and that question was and remains a genuine dispute, because the disease spreads under more than one mode and the relative weight of rodent and human routes has been argued from the pattern of mortality rather than from a specimen. Naming the cause and explaining the epidemic are separate achievements with separate evidence, and a study that claims the second on the strength of the first is exactly the move this item is aimed at.
questions.hint: Ask what the specimen can identify, and what it would take to establish a route.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A reservoir that was looked for and not found
questions.learningObjective: explain what follows from a search for a reservoir that returns nothing
questions.stem: A study tests whether a combination of soil type and rodent community could support a persistent reservoir of the plague organism in a part of Europe, first validating its method by testing it against a region where such reservoirs are known, then applying it to historical and modern data from Europe. It finds no support for a reservoir in Europe and attributes this to a shortage of suitable host species, which is far lower than in the two comparison regions. Which inference is best supported?

options.text: A European absence of a persistent reservoir proves that the disease could never have been present in Europe, since no reservoir means no presence
options.misconception: concludes an absence of the organism from an absence of a reservoir

options.text: The finding shows that the method is faulty, since a method that validates on two regions and returns nothing on a third has shown only that it detects what it was built to detect
options.misconception: dismisses a validated method for a result it did not predict

options.text: The finding shows the shortage of hosts is what limits the disease everywhere, so the comparison regions must have the same shortage
options.misconception: generalises from a regional finding to the regions that contradict it

options.text: A European absence of a persistent reservoir is consistent with the disease having arrived repeatedly from elsewhere, since a population unable to hold the organism would extinguish it between arrivals

questions.explanation: The method's self-validation is what makes the negative result interesting, and it is worth saying why. A test calibrated on regions where the reservoir is known, and returning nothing elsewhere, is not a test that has failed to work; it is a test doing what it was built to do, and the direction of its error is known because the two positive cases bound it. What the result then supports is a specific and useful claim about persistence: a population of hosts too small and too poor to keep the organism alive locally would have to be re-seeded from outside, and that changes the history entirely, since the disease's presence becomes a sequence of arrivals rather than a long-standing condition. The distractors each make a stronger claim than the design supports. A negative result for a habitat is a statement about the habitat, not about the animal, and the fourth option simply contradicts the comparison that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask what a validated method returning nothing is evidence about.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Cases, deaths, and a share of a population
questions.learningObjective: compute proportions from an epidemic report and read what each proportion bears on
questions.stem: A large port city of about 50,000 people records, for one autumn, roughly 11,000 people ill and roughly 5,000 deaths, and a separate return lists about 240 deaths among the population that physicians of the day had believed not liable to the fever. Which evaluation of those figures is best supported?

options.text: The deaths are about one person in ten of the city's people, and the group in question accounts for fewer than one death in twenty of the total, so a belief that spared that group from the measures applied to everyone else was not borne out by the count
The deaths are about one person in five, and the group in question accounts for most of the total, so the belief was contradicted on both counts at once
options.misconception: computes two proportions that neither of the figures supports

options.text: The deaths are about one person in fifty, and the group's figure is large enough to be decisive, so the record shows the belief was sound and the harm came from elsewhere
options.misconception: inverts both ratios and reads the smaller figure as decisive

options.text: The proportions cannot be computed, since the figures are given to the nearest hundred and the population is given to the nearest thousand
options.misconception: treats rounding as though it prevented a proportion from being estimated

questions.explanation: Two proportions have to be computed and both are simple, which is the point of asking for them. Five thousand deaths among a city of about fifty thousand is one death in ten of the people, which is what makes the event a demographic catastrophe as well as a medical one. Two hundred and forty among five thousand is under one in twenty, and it is the more striking figure of the two, because the belief it bears on predicted something near zero: the physicians' opinion was that this population was not liable, and the belief was acted upon by exempting the population from the measures given to everyone else. The last option is a real caution dressed as a refusal, since a figure given to the nearest hundred supports a proportion quoted to the nearest percentage point, and the habit of computing the proportion and then stating the precision it deserves is one of the more useful things a reader can practise.
questions.hint: Compute the deaths as a share of the city, and then the group's share of the deaths.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rate whose denominator changed under it
questions.learningObjective: assess a rate computed across a change in the population it divides by
questions.stem: A study reports that the rate of deaths from a fever in a port city rose from about one per thousand of the population in an ordinary year to about one per hundred in the worst week of an outbreak, and quotes a single population figure for the city taken from the year before. Which problem with the figure is most likely to matter?

options.text: One week is too short a period for a rate to mean anything, since a rate computed over seven days is not comparable with one computed over a year
options.misconception: denies a rate its meaning by an objection to the interval alone

options.text: The figure is a proportion and not a rate, since no time appears in it, and a rate must have a unit per year by definition
options.misconception: insists on one unit of time when several are legitimate

options.text: The population of a port city changes fast in an outbreak, through arrival, flight and displacement, so the denominator in the worst week is not the one that was counted a year earlier
The figure is unusable because the disease was untestable in that period, so the numerator is a count of diagnoses rather than of cases
options.misconception: objects to a numerator the record has already defined for us

questions.explanation: A rate is a ratio and a rate is only as good as both of its halves, and the half that fails quietly in this case is the denominator. A port city in an outbreak is the least stable population in the record: people arrive from an infected district, people with means leave for the country, and whole households are broken up and moved. Every one of those movements changes the count of people at risk, and they do not change it at random, since flight removes the people with the most resources and arrival can bring the people most likely to be exposed. So a numerator collected over a week of upheaval divided by a population counted in calmer circumstances can move a long way in either direction, and the direction is not known without more information. The lesson is general: when a rate's denominator comes from a different time from its numerator, the rate is an estimate with a structural uncertainty, not a measurement.
questions.hint: Ask when the denominator was counted, and what was happening to the population in between.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shock, a harvest, and a departure
questions.learningObjective: separate evidence of a cause from evidence of its consequences

stimulus.body: A study reports four findings about one year in the early nineteenth century: a large eruption in the tropics in the spring, dated by ice cores; a summer in the northern hemisphere with an unusual number of days without a frost and a documented failure of the harvest in several districts; a rise in the price of the main staple grain in those districts; and a rise in the number of people leaving the countryside for the towns. The study adds: 'The last three findings are consistent with one another, and consistency is all that can be claimed. A failed harvest raises the price of grain and sends people away, and many things besides an eruption fail a harvest.'
stimulus.license: original text written for this bank; no protected source reproduced

questions.stem: Read the findings. Which statement about the evidence is best supported?

options.text: All four findings are independent evidence, since a rise in price and a rise in departures cannot be produced by anything except a distant eruption
options.misconception: treats downstream consequences as independent confirmations

options.text: The eruption is irrelevant, since a crop can fail from any cause and the sequence of findings is consistent with a harvest failure alone
options.misconception: dismisses the one dated element of the sequence

options.text: The study overclaims in calling the findings consistent, since four findings that follow from one another are not a consistency at all
options.misconception: objects to a word while accepting that the chain is unconfirmed

options.text: The dated eruption is evidence about cause, the failed harvest is evidence about effect, and the price and the departures are consequences of the harvest rather than independent evidence that the eruption reached the people

questions.explanation: The four findings sit at different distances from the cause, and the value of the study lies in having said so. Only the eruption is dated by an independent physical method, and only the harvest failure is a direct measurement of the thing the eruption is supposed to have done to the world; everything after that is a human response to the harvest. This is not a criticism of the study, which says exactly as much, but it does define what the evidence can bear. A price is a good early-warning indicator and a poor attribution tool, because a price rises for reasons of transport, of policy, of currency and of panic as readily as for a short crop, and a rise in departures from a district is the most indirect evidence of the three because movement responds to wages, to conscription and to a dozen other pressures. The chain is worth mapping; the discipline is in not counting its later links as confirmations of its first.
questions.hint: Ask which findings would still occur if the eruption had not happened, given a failed harvest for some other reason.
